why: Kf5 ignored Rf3+ and left the bishop on f2 pinned and attacked twice.
Qc6 offered a queen trade that removed the d7 queen, the only defender of d6.
Bd6 ignored Bxf6, which exploits the pinned defender of e4, and missed taking on d5.
c5 pushed a pawn to a square attacked twice and defended once, and h6 gains time against Bg5.
Grabbing b2 ignored Qh7+ and Qh8# against a king with no flight square.
Qxd7 pulled the queen off e7, leaving the knight on e5 attacked twice and defended once; Kxd7 kept it.
Bc5 ignored that e5 was undefended against Nxe5; Nc6 defends it while developing.
Bxf3 gave up the bishop pair and doubled nothing for it; retreating to h5 kept the bishop.
Rf4 put the rook where Bg3 hits it with gain of tempo, instead of a calm useful move like b6.
Qf2 walked into Ng4 with tempo and left b2 undefended after the bishop on c1 was tied up.
Bb5 left the king in the centre with lines opening, allowing checks that win the rook; Nc3 develops.
Na5 ignored the b5 break; a5 stops it and keeps the knight off the rim.
Castling ignored the d5 push; Nd4 controls the centre and hits the bishop on f5.
Bf4 avoided the right trade; Bxf6 removes the attacker and the fxg5 threat.
d4 pushed a pawn to a square attacked three times and defended twice; d3 supports the centre safely.
